title: Depart from me (Luke 5:1–11)
hook: after the great catch Peter falls down: I am a sinful man

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus read Isaiah in the Nazareth synagogue: Christos, the anointed one. Your line was good news to the poor.

Fishermen on the lake of Genesareth worked at night, when the fish came up toward the surface. So picture the morning. Simon and his partners have been out all night and caught nothing. They're on the shore, washing their nets, tired and done. A crowd presses in on a teacher, who climbs into Simon's boat and asks him to push off a little, so he can talk to the people from the water. When he's finished, he says what no tired fisherman wants to hear: go back out. Let down your nets again. In the daytime.
screen: `ALL NIGHT, NOTHING.` → `A TEACHER IN SIMON'S BOAT.` → `PUT OUT INTO THE DEEP.`

segments.voice: Simon's answer is honest and a little weary: "Master, we have laboured all the night, and have taken nothing: but at thy word I will let down the net." And the nets fill so full they begin to break. He waves for the other boat, James and John, and both boats load up until they start to sink. You'd expect a fisherman to celebrate. Instead Luke says Simon Peter fell down at Jesus' knees: "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord." It's strange. Nobody accused Peter of anything. But being that close to something holy made him see himself clearly, and what he saw made him want distance. Isaiah felt it in the Temple, crying out that he was a man of unclean lips. Jesus doesn't argue with Peter about whether he's a sinner. He doesn't leave, either. He says: "Fear not: from henceforth thou shalt catch men." Peter asks for distance and gets a job. Then a quiet line: they brought their boats to land, and leaving all things, they followed him. Catholics hear an echo of this at every Mass. Just before Communion, the people say they are not worthy to receive the Lord, and ask him only to say the word. Those words come from a Roman centurion a little later in Luke, but the instinct is Peter's on the beach: I'm not ready for you to come this close. And in both stories, he comes anyway.
screen: `AT THY WORD I WILL LET DOWN THE NET.` · `THE NETS BREAK, THE BOATS SINK.` · `PETER ASKS FOR DISTANCE.` · `FEAR NOT: YOU'LL CATCH PEOPLE.` · then, large: `DEPART FROM ME, FOR I AM A SINFUL MAN.`

segments.voice: Notice one thing in you that makes you want to keep God, or anyone good, at arm's length: a habit, a regret, a mood you're in today. Don't fix it; just name it, the way Peter named his, and then picture the answer he got: not a lecture, just fear not, and an invitation to stay in the boat. If you pray, say Peter's words, and rest in the silence after them.
Genesareth. The lake where Peter's great catch left him saying depart from me, until Jesus answered, fear not. Today's word.
Your line: fear not. The answer Jesus gave to I'm not ready. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke's call of Peter at Sunday Mass in the year Luke's Gospel is read, and before Communion the whole congregation says aloud that they are not worthy, asking the Lord only to say the word.

original.note: Greek: fear not, or stop being afraid. Jesus' answer to Peter in Luke 5:10.

trapdoor: what you thought: Peter asked Jesus to leave because he was annoyed.
what it means: being near the holy showed Peter himself, and he felt unworthy. Jesus answers with fear not and a calling.
what a scholar hears: Luke's word for the catch of men, zogron, means taking alive: it's a net that rescues, not a hook that kills.
recall: Greek: the rising of the sun

chat.says: After the huge catch of fish, why did Peter tell Jesus to go away?
options: Close to something holy, he saw himself clearly and felt he was a sinner.
He was angry that a teacher had told an expert fisherman how to fish.
He was afraid the boats would sink and wanted Jesus safely on shore.
chat.meaning: Peter fell at his knees: depart from me, for I am a sinful man. Jesus didn't argue or leave; he said fear not.

Genesareth.meaning: the lake where Simon and his partners fished

Isaiah.meaning: the prophet who cried out in the Temple: a man of unclean lips
